hops.title: Watch the veins on your hand fill and empty
hops.text: Sit down and let one hand hang loosely at your side for half a minute. If the veins on the back of that hand show at all, they plump up: the column of blood above them adds a little pressure, and their thin, compliant walls stretch to hold extra blood. Now lift the hand slowly toward your chest and a little higher. The veins flatten and almost disappear as blood drains out of them. In one study, they emptied with less lift in people lying flat than in people sitting up. This is a demonstration of compliance, not a health check.

sources.citation: Shykoff BE, Hawari FI, Izzo JL Jr. Diameter, pressure and compliance relationships in dorsal hand veins. Vascular Medicine 6(2):97-102 (2001).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student at a desk lets one arm hang down and raises the other hand to chest height, looking at the back of the raised hand.
image.caption: Thin, compliant veins fill when the hand hangs low and empty when it is lifted.

hops.title: Why astronauts get puffy faces
hops.text: Spaceflight doctors have a name for the look astronauts get in orbit: "puffy face, bird legs." Without gravity pulling fluid toward the feet, it shifts toward the chest and head, bringing round cheeks, stuffy noses and thinner legs. To find out why, NASA researchers tilted seven volunteers six degrees head-down for eight hours, a way to mimic weightlessness on the ground, and measured all four Starling pressures. By hour eight, capillary pressure in the lower lip had risen from 27.7 to 33.9 mmHg. By hour four, plasma oncotic pressure had fallen from 21.5 to 18.2 mmHg. More push out plus less pull in favors filtration, and the volunteers' faces swelled.

sources.citation: Mendes Zambetta R, Signini EF, Ocamoto GN, et al. Frontiers in Physiology 15:1438089 (2024).

Parazynski SE, Hargens AR, Tucker B, Aratow M, Styf J, Crenshaw A. Transcapillary fluid shifts in tissues of the head and neck during and after simulated microgravity. Journal of Applied Physiology 71(6):2469-2475 (1991).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A cheerful astronaut with round, puffy cheeks and thin legs floats in a space station cabin beside a window showing Earth.
image.caption: In orbit fluid shifts headward; a ground study showed how that tips Starling's balance toward swelling.

hops.afterHeading: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals
hops.title: A blizzard, a milk can and the discovery behind warfarin
hops.text: In a February 1933 blizzard, Wisconsin farmer Ed Carlson drove 190 miles to Madison with a dead heifer, a pile of moldy feed and a milk can full of blood that would not clot. He was looking for the state veterinarian and wandered into biochemist Karl Paul Link's lab instead. The culprit was spoiled sweet clover hay. Link's team traced it to dicoumarol, which forms from the clover's coumarin as it spoils and counters vitamin K, leaving less working prothrombin, the precursor of thrombin. A lab-made cousin became a rat poison Link named warfarin, after the Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation, and later a widely prescribed blood thinner.

sources.citation: Ball CM, Featherstone PJ. Anaesthesia and Intensive Care 53(3):148-150 (2025), on the history of dicoumarol and warfarin.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage metal milk can and a bundle of dried clover hay on snowy steps outside a brick university building.
image.caption: Spoiled sweet clover led to dicoumarol, and a related compound became the blood thinner warfarin.

audio.title: A pale fish, a corrected textbook and a working leech
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about blood and the vessels that carry it: a fish with blood so pale it looks almost like water, a famous textbook that dismissed an old anatomist's report, and a small animal that surgeons still put to work.

Start in the Southern Ocean around Antarctica, in water close to the freezing point of seawater. The crocodile icefish lives there, and its blood is nearly colorless. Icefish are the only known vertebrates that make no hemoglobin at all. Oxygen simply dissolves in their plasma, so their blood carries only about a tenth of the oxygen that a red-blooded relative's does. To make up for it, an icefish has an enlarged heart and an extended network of vessels, and it pumps a large volume of blood. Losing red cells does make the blood thinner and easier to pump, milliliter for milliliter. But an icefish pumps so much more blood that its heart seems to use more energy overall than the heart of a similar-sized red-blooded relative. The icefish gets by rather than wins. Part of how it gets by is radius. In two icefish species, the average muscle capillary radius was about one and a half times as large as in the red-blooded relatives studied. Now use Poiseuille's law on an ideal tube: make it that much wider and keep its length and the fluid the same. One and a half to the fourth power is about five, so the wider tube offers about one fifth as much resistance.

The second story is about a correction that took two centuries. In seventeen eighty-seven, the Italian anatomist Paolo Mascagni described lymphatic vessels in the coverings of the brain, and he helped direct the making of wax anatomical models for the Josephinum in Vienna. Much later, the thirty-eighth edition of Gray's Anatomy suggested that Mascagni was so taken with the lymphatic system that he saw lymph vessels where there were none, in the brain. For generations, the standard view was that the brain had no lymphatic vessels. Then in twenty fifteen, two independent teams working in mice found them: lymphatic vessels in the dura, the tough outer membrane around the brain, running alongside its large veins and carrying fluid and immune cells to lymph nodes in the neck. Whether Mascagni saw those same vessels is still debated, because some of what he drew may have been other thread-like tissue. So the brain tissue itself still has none, but in mice, at least, its outer covering does, and the old dismissal of lymphatics around the brain was wrong.

Last, a surgery ward. In two thousand four, the U S Food and Drug Administration cleared live medicinal leeches as a medical device. Surgeons still use them when the veins of a tissue graft are congested and blood backs up in the tissue. The leech works on the last step of the clotting cascade from this lesson. Its saliva carries hirudin, named in nineteen oh four, and the strongest natural blocker of thrombin found so far. Without thrombin, fibrinogen is not turned into fibrin, so fibrin forms slowly at the bite. The bite can keep bleeding after the leech lets go, which gives the backed-up blood another way out.

A pale fish, a textbook that had to be corrected, and a hard-working leech: the same rules of resistance, drainage and clotting, turning up in places you might not expect.
